764.title: the dice game
764.hook: Duryodhana walks through Maya's hall, mistakes floor for water and water for floor, and hears laughter
764.howItsDone: Some Hindu storytellers treat Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall as the opening of the dice-game story, the small wound that leads to the great quarrel.

segments.voice: Yesterday a light rose from Shishupala and entered Krishna, and the Rajasuya was finished. Where you'd rather turn that light.

The guests have gone home, but one has stayed behind. Duryodhana lingers at Indraprastha with his uncle Shakuni, wandering through the great hall the asura builder Maya made for the Pandavas. It's a hall of wonders, and wonders can be tricky. Floors that look like water. Water that looks like floor. Doors that seem open and aren't. A new story starts here, the dice game. But it doesn't start with dice. It starts with a man walking through a beautiful room and getting it wrong, again and again.
screen: `ONE GUEST STAYS BEHIND.` → `MAYA'S HALL OF WONDERS.` → `IT STARTS WITHOUT DICE.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Duryodhana comes to a spot on the floor that looks like a pool. It's crystal, but he takes it for water and gathers up his clothes to wade across. Nothing wet. Then he comes to a real pool, so clear it looks like solid floor, and walks straight in, clothes and all. And here's the line that hurts: Bhima sees it, and laughs. The servants laugh too. Yudhishthira, the host, sends him dry clothes. It doesn't help. A little further on, Duryodhana tries to walk through a doorway that looks open, and strikes his head on a wall of crystal. At another door, which really is open, he holds back, thinking it closed. By the end of his visit, the hall has fooled him over and over, and his mistakes have had an audience. Hold onto this, because it's small, and it's going to be enormous. Nobody attacked Duryodhana. Nobody planned this. A beautiful building and a little laughter. But he has just watched kings from near and far bring gifts to his cousin, and now his cousin's house has made him look like a fool. The poem doesn't excuse what he does next. It shows the moment the wound opens. The dice game will look like a game of chance, but its roots are here: a man walking alone through a room that made him feel small, with laughter behind him.

segments.voice: Recall a moment you laughed at someone's mistake, even kindly: a wrong turn, a spill, a slip of the tongue. Now see it from their side, the heat in the face, the wish to disappear, and let both views sit side by side without guilt. If you pray, you can remember them kindly in your prayer; if not, simply wish them ease.

765.title: the dice game
765.hook: on the road home, Duryodhana tells Shakuni what is eating him, and Shakuni offers a way to win without a war
765.carry: name the sting before it becomes a plan
765.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings of the Mahabharata, Shakuni is known as the master of the dice, and the conversation on the road is told as the moment Duryodhana's envy becomes a plan.

segments.voice: Yesterday the dice game began without dice: Duryodhana fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at. Help before you laugh.

Duryodhana is heading home to Hastinapura, and he keeps sighing. His uncle Shakuni, riding with him, notices and asks what's wrong. And Duryodhana tells him. Not a polite version. The whole thing: the kings bowing to his cousin, the wealth flowing in, the hall that made a fool of him, the laughter. He says he can't bear it. He says it's burning him up inside. A confession on the road, and an uncle who hears in it an opportunity.
screen: `SIGHING ON THE ROAD HOME.` → `SHAKUNI ASKS.` → `THE WHOLE THING POURS OUT.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Duryodhana actually says. Not that the Pandavas cheated, or wronged him. That they're prospering, and he can't stand it. Their success is the injury. That's envy in its plainest form, and the poem lets him say it out loud, without dressing it up. Shakuni listens, and at first does what a good friend might. Don't grieve, he says; the Pandavas have their good fortune and you have yours. But Duryodhana won't be comforted. So Shakuni changes course. You can't beat them in battle, he says in effect; they're too strong. But there's another way. Yudhishthira loves to play dice, and he doesn't play well. I do. Invite him to a game, and I'll win everything he has, and you won't have to lift a weapon. Clever, and dark. A war would be open; everyone would see who attacked whom. A game looks friendly. It has rules. The loser agreed to play. Shakuni is offering a way to take a kingdom and keep your hands clean. And notice who starts this. Not a monster from a cartoon. A hurting man, and an uncle who knows exactly where it hurts. The dice game is born on this road, out of envy spoken aloud and a plan offered in reply.

766.title: the dice game
766.hook: Duryodhana and Shakuni work on the blind king, a hall is built for the game, and Vidura's warning goes unheeded
766.carry: let a worry change one thing
766.howItsDone: In Hindu retellings, Vidura is remembered as a voice of wise counsel at the Kuru court, the one who tells the blind king what he doesn't want to hear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the road home, Duryodhana spoke his envy aloud, and Shakuni offered a plan to win without a war. Name the sting before it becomes a plan.

A plan needs permission. Duryodhana is a prince, not the king. To invite Yudhishthira to anything, the invitation has to come from his father, Dhritarashtra, the blind king of Hastinapura. So uncle and nephew go to the palace. Shakuni speaks first, gently, about how pale and thin the prince has grown. And the king, who loves his son, asks him what's wrong. The plan moves from a road to a throne room, and a father has to decide.
screen: `A PLAN NEEDS PERMISSION.` → `TO THE BLIND KING.` → `A FATHER ASKS WHAT'S WRONG.`

segments.voice: Duryodhana tells his father what he told Shakuni: the Pandavas' wealth, the kings at their feet, the hall that shamed him. And Shakuni lays out the game. Dhritarashtra hesitates. In the telling, he wants to ask Vidura first, his wise half-brother, whose counsel he trusts. Duryodhana pushes back hard, in effect: ask Vidura, and Vidura will stop it, and I'll be lost. He presses until his father gives way. So the king orders a splendid new hall built for the game, worthy of the guests. Only then does he call Vidura, not to ask whether, but to tell him. Vidura says plainly that he doesn't approve. This game, he warns, will set the cousins against each other and end in quarrel. Dhritarashtra doesn't change course. If the gods are kind, he answers, no harm will come; what is fated will happen. Then he gives Vidura a job: go to Indraprastha, and bring Yudhishthira here to play. Look at that. The one man who sees the danger clearly is sent to deliver the invitation. A father who couldn't say no to his son has made the counselor he trusts most the messenger of the thing he warned against. The poem doesn't call Dhritarashtra wicked. It shows a man who heard the warning, and loved his son too much to act on it.

767.title: the dice game
767.hook: before the first throw, Yudhishthira calls the game deceit, Shakuni dares him, and he plays anyway
767.howItsDone: The dice scene is retold in homes, on stage and on screen, and the talk before the first throw is a place where readers and listeners stop to argue about Yudhishthira's choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday the blind king had a hall built for the game, and sent Vidura, who had warned against it, to carry the invitation. Let a worry change one thing.

The new hall is ready, and Yudhishthira has come. The guests are seated, the cloth is spread, and the dice are out. Before anyone throws, there's a conversation, and it's easy to hurry past it on the way to the drama. Don't. Everything that follows is already folded inside it. Yudhishthira says plainly what he thinks of this kind of game. Shakuni answers him, and the answer has a hook in it. And a choice gets made in the open, before the elders have even taken their seats.
screen: `THE BOARD IS SET.` → `A CONVERSATION FIRST.` → `A CHOICE MADE IN THE OPEN.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Shakuni opens: the hall is full; it's time to play. Yudhishthira doesn't pretend. Gambling of this kind is deceit, he says; there's no warrior's courage in it. Don't beat us by crooked means. Shakuni's answer is clever. Every contest is one person knowing more than another. A skilled player beats an unskilled one, a learned person beats one who isn't, and nobody calls that cheating. Then the sting: if you're afraid, don't play. Yudhishthira's reply is the hinge of the whole episode. Called to play, I don't turn back; that's my vow. And fate rules everyone. So he asks who he'll be playing against. Duryodhana answers: I'll put up the wealth, and my uncle Shakuni will throw for me. Yudhishthira sees the problem at once. One man playing with another's stake seems to him against the rules. But if that's how they want it, let it begin. In a few lines, he named the danger and the unfairness, was told that refusing would look like fear, and walked forward anyway, holding a vow and a belief about fate. Some readers call that integrity. Others call it pride. The poem gives both something to hold. The elders come in and take their seats, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Vidura among them, with heavy hearts, the poem says. Yudhishthira puts down his first stake, a costly pearl set in gold. Shakuni throws. And he wins.

768.title: the dice game
768.hook: stake after stake, the same short line: I have won; and Vidura warns that the winner is in danger too
768.howItsDone: Vidura's warnings in the dice hall are a place where teachers and storytellers often pause, and his image of the honey-gatherer is retold as a picture of desire that can't see its own danger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the talk before the first throw: a warning, a dare, a vow, and a pearl set in gold, lost. Ask whose voice that is.
screen: `CALLED TO PLAY, I DON'T TURN BACK.`

segments.voice: There's a line in this part of the poem that keeps coming back, like a drumbeat. Yudhishthira names a stake. Shakuni throws. And then Shakuni says, in effect: I have won. Then again. And again. The poem repeats it until the words themselves begin to sound like a warning. And one man in the hall stands up and tries to stop it.
screen: `A LINE LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` → `I HAVE WON.` → `ONE MAN TRIES TO STOP IT.`

segments.voice: After the pearl, Yudhishthira reaches for the next stake. Treasure. Gold. A fine chariot. Servants. Elephants. Horses. Soldiers. Each time he describes what he's putting down, carefully, almost proudly, as if the quality of the stake could change the fall of the dice. Each time the throw goes to Shakuni, and the same short sentence follows: I have won. That refrain takes the suspense away. We stop asking who will win the throw, and start asking something harder: why doesn't he stop? Somebody in the hall asks it out loud. Vidura, the blind king's wise half-brother, turns to Dhritarashtra. In the telling, he gives him a picture. A man climbs high after honey, so taken with the honey that he doesn't see the fall in front of him. That, Vidura says, is your son with the dice. He begs the king to stop the game while there's still a family left to save. Duryodhana answers with scorn. He accuses Vidura of always speaking for the other side, against the very family that shelters him. And Dhritarashtra says nothing that stops the game. Here's what's striking. Vidura's honey picture isn't about Yudhishthira, the one losing. It's about Duryodhana, the one winning. In the poem's eyes, the winner is in danger too. Each throw won for him is a step nearer the edge, and he can't see it, because his hands are full of honey.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dice game: stake after stake, the drumbeat of I have won, and Vidura's man reaching for honey.

Every treasure is gone. In the telling, Yudhishthira stakes his herds, his lands, his city, even the ornaments the princes wear. Lost, every one. And then the game changes from a matter of things to a matter of people. Shakuni asks: is there anything left? There is. Sitting near Yudhishthira, listening to all of it, are his four brothers.
screen: `EVERY TREASURE IS GONE.` → `IS THERE ANYTHING LEFT?` → `HIS FOUR BROTHERS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira stakes Nakula, one of the twins. Shakuni throws, and wins. He stakes the other twin, Sahadeva. Lost. Then Shakuni tries something sly. The twins, he says, are Madri's sons. Surely Bhima and Arjuna, Kunti's sons, your own mother's sons, are dearer to you. You won't stake them. It's an attempt to split the brothers along their mothers' line. And Yudhishthira, losing everything, still catches it. In effect: you're trying to divide us, and that's wrong. Then, as if to show they can't be divided, he stakes Arjuna. Lost. He stakes Bhima. Lost. He stakes himself. Lost. Shakuni says one stake is left: Draupadi. And Yudhishthira stakes her, describing her goodness as he does. Now the poem turns to the room. The elders, Bhishma, Drona and Kripa, are shaken; the telling says they break into a sweat. Vidura holds his head in his hands. The blind king, who can't see the board, keeps asking whether the throw has been won. Shakuni throws, and he wins. Look at the strange shape of that last streak. Yudhishthira's loyalty to his brothers is real; he won't let Shakuni set them against each other. And that same loyalty is what he puts on the board, one brother after another. A virtue and a disaster in the same breath. The stakes run out here, with a woman lost in a game she never sat down to play.

770.howItsDone: Draupadi's question is retold in homes, dance and theater, and it's discussed by readers and commentators as a question about dharma and law that the epic leaves open.

segments.voice: Yesterday the last stakes fell: the twins, Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira himself, and then Draupadi. A week that ran from Duryodhana's stumble in Maya's hall to the last stake in the dice hall. Your line was name it plainly, the way he did.

The game is over, and Duryodhana wants Draupadi brought into the hall. First he tells Vidura to fetch her. Vidura refuses flatly. In the telling, he says she can't have become anyone's slave, because Yudhishthira staked her after he'd already lost himself. Hold on to that; it's the thread of everything that follows. So Duryodhana turns to an usher, a servant whose job is carrying messages, and sends him to the women's rooms.
screen: `VIDURA REFUSES TO FETCH HER.` → `HE LOST HIMSELF FIRST.` → `A MESSENGER AT HER DOOR.`

segments.voice: The usher tells Draupadi what has happened: Yudhishthira, carried away by the game, has lost her to Duryodhana, and she must come. Draupadi doesn't come. She sends him back to put one thing to the gambler in the hall: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? It's a precise question. If he lost himself first, he was no longer free when he staked her, and perhaps had nothing left to stake. If he staked her first, the answer is different. She isn't pleading. She's asking for the facts the whole claim rests on. The usher asks it in the hall. And Yudhishthira says nothing. The telling says he sits as if he's lost his senses, and answers not a word, good or bad. Duryodhana tells the usher: let her come here and ask it herself. The usher goes back, uneasy, and Draupadi sends him again, this time with a question for everyone: ask the assembly what is right for me to do, and I'll do it. First it was for one man. Now it's for a whole hall of kings and elders. The usher, caught between a furious prince and a woman who won't be moved, hesitates to go a third time. So Duryodhana sends his brother Duhshasana instead. The question, still unanswered, is about to walk into the hall in person.
